title: Acetree Retail — Runtime routing, model selection, and tool-calling discovery
summary: Discovery call to understand Acetree's latency/cost targets, multilingual catalog generation use case, need for long context (50k tokens), and tool-calling to inventory/order systems. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC), SOC2/KMS needs, and next steps for benchmarks and security docs.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Tom Harris (Head of ML, Acetree), Priya Nair (Platform Eng, Acetree), Luca Romano (CTO, Acetree)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro from our side — I'm Maya, I run the account, and Diego is our solutions engineer, he'll walk through model/runtime choices.
[00:12] Tom: Hi all, Tom here. We're trying to decide between Redwood hosted vs reserving Dedicated GPUs vs a private VPC deploy. Main drivers: latency under 200ms for short responses, occasionally need very long context for batch catalog ingest (20k-50k tokens), and must support FR/ES/EN/JA output. Also we need tool calling to our inventory and order APIs.
[00:35] Diego: Great — that maps to what we usually see. A couple quick questions: are the long-context requests primarily generation for product descriptions and merchandising, or are they retrieval+generate flows?
[00:45] Tom: Mostly retrieval + generate. We'll chunk catalogs but want the model to see up to a full seasonal catalog when writing summaries; so sometimes it's 40k tokens. Latency not critical on those long ones, but cost matters.
[01:05] Priya: On security — we need SOC2, SSO with SAML, and KMS for keys. We also prefer audit logs to be shipped to our SIEM. Can Redwood do that on hosted?
[01:20] Maya: Hosted covers SOC2 and we provide audit logs; for KMS and customer-managed keys, that's typically Private (VPC) or Dedicated with customer key options depending on the plan. We can share the security pack after this call.
[01:34] Luca: I want to understand routing: can critical low-latency endpoints be pinned to a dedicated pool while non-critical batch jobs go to hosted? We want cost control but SLAs on our checkout flows.
[01:48] Diego: Yes, that's a common hybrid. Redwood supports policy-based routing — you can route by route, by latency SLO, or by model. For example, pin checkout to a Dedicated pool with reserved GPUs and route batch catalog tasks to hosted or a cheaper quantized variant.
[02:05] Tom: Okay, model selection. We're evaluating open models — one candidate is an LLaMA-derivative with 70B weights, another is a 13B with 32k context. We care about multilingual quality and tool-calling reliability. Any recommendations?
[02:25] Diego: For multilingual and tool-calling, bigger context length and instruction-tuned models win. But there's a tradeoff between model size and latency/cost. For high throughput, a 13B with 32k context that's quantized can give decent quality and low cost. For best quality in EN+JA, a 70B or 30B with proper finetune/llm-adapter might be needed. Redwood can host multiple model variants and do automated fallback — e.g., try 13B for normal traffic, failover to 30B for complex queries.
[02:50] Priya: How deterministic is tool-calling? We can't have accidental API calls during evaluation. Need strict filters and a way to sandbox tool execution.
[03:02] Diego: We surface explicit tool-calling APIs and function schemas. You can require a two-step: first the model returns a structured call (JSON), then your router/SE validates before executing. We can also run simulator checks in a sandbox.
[03:18] Tom: Cool. On context length — you mentioned 32k and 50k — does Redwood support >32k windows easily? And what's the cost/per-token like?
[03:29] Maya: We do support longer contexts. Pricing depends on model variant and token accounting, and longer contexts increase memory and compute. For extremely long contexts we also recommend prefix caching and retrieval augmentation to avoid sending the entire catalog every request. Diego can follow up with cost examples.
[03:45] Diego: Yep, prefix/KV cache is key. For catalog workflows we suggest embedding-based retrieval + KV cache for hot prefixes. That reduces per-request tokens and keeps latency low. Quantized models with a dedicated pool can run longer sequences more cheaply.
[04:05] Luca: Any recommendations on open models for multilingual e‑commerce? We were looking at Mistral variants and some community LLAMAs.
[04:14] Diego: Mistral-like models are strong, but you'll need to test on product copy and JP content. We maintain performance profiles for verified open models and can run evals on your prompt set. We often compare Anthropic-open, Mistral, Meta derivatives and tuned Llama-derivs.
[04:32] Tom: Speaking of Anthropic/OpenAI — we still might use them for certain safety-critical flows. Will Redwood let us route to external APIs as fallback?
[04:42] Diego: Yes, policy routing can call external endpoints; you can set cost vs latency rules. Note outbound costs and data residency implications.
[04:52] Priya: Ok, compliance — if we go Dedicated, can keys stay in our KMS? We need HSM-backed key support for PII flows.
[05:03] Maya: Dedicated and Private support customer-managed KMS. For HSM-backed keys we have integrations — we'll include a KMS/HSM matrix in the security doc.
[05:15] Tom: Let's talk about a POC. Ideally we run: 1) a small host benchmark (hosted 13B quantized) for throughput/latency, 2) a dedicated pool trial for checkout latency, and 3) a longer context eval with a 50k token pipeline. Can Redwood run synthetic benchmarks?
[05:34] Diego: Yes, we can execute benchmarks against test inputs you provide. For the 50k workflow we'll likely recommend retrieval+condense to keep compute reasonable. We can also provide a managed POC with a sandbox VPC.
[05:50] Luca: Pricing sensitivity — what's ballpark for a dedicated pool with 4xH100-like capacity?
[05:58] Maya: Ballpark depends on reserved term and region; we'll send an indicative quote. To avoid surprises we'll include unit economics examples (cost per 1k tokens at different batch sizes and sequence lengths).
[06:12] Tom: Questions from our side: 1) how are model updates and rollouts managed? 2) What's the monitoring surface for hallucination/regression?
[06:22] Diego: Rollouts: versioned model catalog with canary/A-B and automatic fallback policies. Monitoring: per-route token costs, latency, and we support quality evals tied to prompts — regression alerts when outputs diverge beyond thresholds. You can hook tracing and diff checks.
[06:40] Priya: Any gotchas for on-prem private deployments? Our infra team is worried about upgrades and patching.
